# 饮食·烹饪·味道 {.unnumbered}



> 本主题共 7 篇语境短文。每篇把一批旧词织进一个场景：**左栏**读短文（目标词加粗），**右栏**常驻该篇生词释义，可先猜后对照。



### A Day in the Kitchen

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
The morning shift at the bistro began quietly. The **chef** tied back her hair in a neat **bun** and scanned the prep list. First she reached for the **wok**, set it over high heat, and let a spoonful of **lard** melt until it shimmered. Into the pan went **dice**d tofu, a splash of **soy** sauce, and a handful of sliced **kale** and **choy**, their leaves wilting in seconds. She added cubes of roasted **yam**, a pinch of **chia** seeds, and a scoop of cooked **sago** pearls for texture—an odd combination, but it worked.

While the stir-fry rested, she moved to the bread station. A tray of **rye** rolls and honey-glazed **nut** loaves was already rising beside a rack of plain **bun**s. She brushed each one with **mel**—pure, amber honey straight from the jar—then slid them into the **oven**. The kitchen filled with a warm, yeasty smell.

For the afternoon menu she planned a light **deli** spread. A **bean** salad dressed with **lime** juice and **mint** sat next to a **plum** and **rosé** reduction that was just **tart** enough to cut through the richness of the cured meats. She would **sear** each slice of duck breast until the skin crackled, then rest it on a bed of **hash** made from root vegetables. On the side: a shot glass of cold **gin**, a thimble of **vin** rouge, and a small dish of **chow** for the staff tasting.

She sliced a lemon, let it **boil** briefly in sugar syrup for a garnish, and stepped back. Tonight they would **dine** well. The **coco** cream dessert was chilling, the **chia**-**sago** pudding was set, and every dish on the pass told the same quiet story: someone had paid attention.

### The Sunday Kitchen

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
The morning begins with a quiet ritual. She halves an **onion** and sets it in a pan already shimmering with oil, then **saute**s the slices until they caramelize and fill the apartment with a deep, smoky **aroma**. Into the same pan go two cans of **clams**, a generous pinch of **cumin**, and a torn **chile** — dried, rust-red, fierce. A rich **sauce** takes shape as the liquids reduce, and she pauses to **savor** every shift in color, nudging the heat up just enough to keep things **crisp** at the edges without burning. On the counter, a slab of **tuna** **filet** waits beside a small bowl of sliced **beets**, their vivid purple already bleeding into the cutting board. She'll **grill** the fish in a few minutes — but first she needs to finish the **bento** she's packing for later: a tidy compartment of rice seasoned with **spice**, another filled with roasted **pecan** halves and sliced **mango**, a third with two fat **prune**s for sweetness.

Meanwhile, the oven holds something more indulgent. A batch of **donut** **dough** is resting on the lower rack — soft and pillowy, waiting for the hot oil and the cloud of powdered sugar. On the shelf above it sits a **bagel** tray, the tops already burnished gold. The **dairy** shelf in the fridge holds the **icing** she'll pipe once things cool: cream cheese thinned with a splash of milk, flecked with **peach** zest. A single **mazer** — a broad, shallow cup salvaged from a flea market — stands ready for warm cider. By noon the kitchen is a cheerful wreck of crumbs and colour, a Saturday **binge** of cooking that started as a plan to **cater** a small gathering and quietly became something larger. She checks the **menus** she sketched last night, crosses off the last item, and ladles soup into a bowl, breaking a **yolk** over the top so it slowly bleeds gold into the broth. She lifts the bowl with both hands and drinks with a long, contented **slurp**.

### A Sunday Kitchen in Full Swing

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
The morning begins at the **pantry**, where jars of **barley**, **quinoa**, and **grains** line the lower shelf alongside a tin of **canned** chickpeas. From those chickpeas comes a bowl of **hummus**, stirred smooth with a wooden **spoon** and finished with a drizzle of **citrus** oil squeezed from a ripe **orange**. On the chopping board, a fistful of **chives** and a crisp stalk of **celery** wait to be scattered over the top — bright, **edible** garnishes that lift the whole thing. Nearby, **prunes** and **pecans** sit ready for the grain salad, and a halved **papaya** spills its coral flesh onto the board, its tropical sweetness a quiet contrast to the **spicy** harissa blended into the dressing.

The main kitchen is louder. A thick **steak** hisses in a cast-iron pan while a pair of **bangers** blister beside it; a soft **omelet** folds over **radish** slivers and wilted herbs in a second skillet. The **buffet** counter is already filling: a pot of **mussel**s steamed open in white wine, a small crock of **caviar** resting on ice, and a platter of **durian** wedges for the brave — a fruit whose reputation far outruns its subtlety. A bottle of maple **syrup** stands next to a stack of blinis meant to carry spoonfuls of roe, and a dish of **taffy** sits at one end for anyone with a sweet tooth.

The **entree** that anchors the table is simpler than it sounds: a warm grain bowl with roasted vegetables, dressed lightly so nothing smothers the honest flavour of each element. The cook wipes her hands on a **napkin**, adjusts the garnish of **pecans**, and steps back to judge the spread. It is a meal built for a curious **palate** — something tart and **citrus**-bright, something **spicy**, something rich enough to need a pause. The kitchen has done its job; now it's up to whoever sits down to **forage** through the plates.

### A Kitchen Saturday, From Morning to Dusk

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
The day begins gently. She stirs a bowl of **granola** and scatters a handful of **raisin**s on top, then pours a thin thread of cream from the **creamer**. The coffee is single-origin **arabica**, brewed in a small ceramic pot — the art of **brewing** unhurried on a weekend morning. Beside the mug sits a shallow **saucer** faintly ringed with yesterday's tea.

By midday the kitchen has warmed into something serious. She pulls out a dog-eared **recipe** and lays ingredients across the counter: fat slices of **salmon**, a coil of **salami**, two **rasher**s of bacon for the pan, and a handful of **shrimp** still faintly pink from the market. A wedge of **avocado** sits next to a pot of thickening cheese — she'd stirred **rennet** into warm milk the night before and left it to set. From the crisper she rescues a pale **turnip** and a few **collard** leaves, the kind of honest vegetables that anchor a pot without announcing themselves. She dusts everything with a **spiced** rub — cumin, smoked paprika, a little black pepper — and watches the **grilled** edges of the salmon go dark gold in the pan. **Starch** from the potato slices crisps against the hot iron. Somewhere in the back of the oven, a pan of **beignet** dough is waiting its turn.

The afternoon drifts toward the larger table. Her brother has taken over the far end, assembling a **burrito** the size of a small log. A **wiener** occupies one small boy's plate with the authority of a state occasion. The **haddock** — poached, not fried, a concession to her father's digestion — rests quietly in a pale broth. A bowl of **apricot** halves, amber and glossy, stands in for dessert. Someone opens a bottle of **Bourbon** and pours small amounts for the adults. The **caterer** hired for the evening's dinner party has just arrived, wheeling a cart through the side door; she works the **canteen** tap to fill her own water bottle before the formalities begin.

Dusk brings the final flourish. The table is the full record of a day's effort — the **cuisine** is nothing fixed, nothing national, just accumulated care. There is **relish** in small jars, amber and green. A tray of cold cuts includes another curl of **salami** and a sliced **wiener** for the stragglers. The **canning** jars of last summer's tomatoes have finally been cracked open, their lids sighing. Someone's **tiffin** tin from lunch is still unwashed by the sink, a mild reproach. It doesn't matter. The meal goes on.

### A Market Stall, a Kitchen, a Table

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
The morning catch arrived early — a whole **halibut** laid flat beside a bucket of silver **herring** and a crate of **mussels** still dripping with salt water. At the next stall, a fishmonger split a live **lobster** down the middle with one clean stroke, while a paper cone of smoked **sardine** drew a small crowd with its sharp, **pungent** perfume.

Back in the kitchen, the prep cook moved with quiet efficiency. She blanched **broccoli** and **spinach** together, then set a pot of **lentils** and mixed **legumes** to simmer low. A tangle of **lettuce** went into cold water to crisp. For the centerpiece, she was making a **risotto** folded with earthy **truffle** shavings — the kind of dish that needed nothing more than a knob of butter and patience. Beside the stove sat jars of dried **oregano** and **parsley**, a tin of ground **mustard**, and a small bottle of pure **vanilla** extract for the dessert course. A handful of **raisins** and diced **mangoes** waited in a bowl nearby, soon to become a compote sharp enough from **morello** cherries to cut through the richness of the main.

The **platter** that went out to the dining room held **sausage** twisted from **poultry** trim, roasted **pumpkin** wedges glazed with honey, and a thin slice of dark **stuffed** bread pressed with dried herbs. **Aromatic** steam rose off everything. The table drinks were simple: a glass of **Seltzer** for those who wanted something clean, a pour of aged **whiskey** for those who did not. Someone asked for a tobacco pouch out of habit, then thought better of it, reaching instead for the last **beverage** on the tray — a cold **truffle**-free herbal infusion, mild and bright.
:::

### A Kitchen in Full Swing

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
The afternoon light fell warm across the counter as she laid out her **culinary** mise en place: a bowl of dried **chickpea**s she'd soaked overnight, a bunch of **scallion**s, a fat **zucchini**, a handful of roasted **hazelnut**s, and a cluster of **asparagus** snapped at the bend. She reached for the **saucepan**, poured in a glug of olive oil, and coaxed the scallions soft before adding the chickpeas and a pinch of **cinnamon** — an old trick that kept the dish from tasting flat. A strip of **plantain** went into a second pan, frying to gold while she folded a herb **omelette** loaded with **cilantro** and a single sliced **scallops**. The **stuffing** for the **casserole** — breadcrumbs, **artichoke** hearts, and a full **teaspoon** of smoked paprika — sat waiting in its bowl, nothing **unsavory** about it.

Before the main event, she set out a small **appetizer** spread: cold **macaroni** tossed in lemon, charred **asparagus** spears beside a ramekin of aioli sparked with **jalapeno**, and a half-eaten pile of **munchies** — spiced crackers she'd been grazing on all morning. A glass of **champagne** stood half-full near the hob, and a single shot of **espresso** cooled forgotten beside it. She lifted a cold **Guinness** for her husband, who was already at the table, turning a **doughnut** in his hands with the focused reverence of a man **savoring** the last one in the box.

For the children there were **Popsicle**s pulled from the freezer and one shared **lollipop** — a concession — and a small cup of **honeydew** wedges to make the meal feel balanced. She ate standing, a **chopstick** in each hand, working through the casserole straight from the dish, grateful for a kitchen that smelled this good.
:::

### A Morning at the Market, an Evening at the Table

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="57%"}
The weekend farmers' market always started the same way: a warm **croissant** torn open at the paper bag, its layers still crackling, eaten standing beside a stall heaped with fruit. She loaded her basket with a ripe **cantaloupe**, a punnet of **raspberry**, a handful of **nectarine**, a small bag of **pistachio**, and two fat **pomegranate** whose skins had just begun to crack. On the next table she found the citrus section — **grapefruit** the size of softballs, and a mesh net of bright **tangerine** that left her fingers smelling of zest. **Coriander** came in tied bunches next to the **green bean**, and she grabbed a firm head of **cauliflower** because it photographed well and roasted even better.

Back in the kitchen, she spread a **place-mat** on the counter and laid out the afternoon's work. The recipe called for onions **caramelize**d low and slow until **glutinous** and amber, then folded into a sauce made rich with a spoonful of **mayonnaise** and a drizzle of oil — no butter, she reminded herself; the jar of **margarine** would do for her **vegetarian** guest. She had picked up smoked paprika from the **delicatessen** around the corner along with a rotisserie **chicken wing** platter for the rest of the table. On the back burner, a small pot held a syrup of **refined sugar** and pomegranate juice slowly reducing toward a glaze.

The drinks were her favorite part to arrange. A craft **Margarita** — **distilled** from good blanco tequila sourced from a local **distiller** who ran something close to a one-man **microbrewery** for agave spirits — waited in a salt-rimmed glass. She set out a pitcher of **refreshment**: cold hibiscus water with thin slices of **nectarine** floating on top. The **succulent** fruit curled at the edges like little boats. She had almost skipped the dessert plate, then remembered the **Croissant-beignet** she'd impulse-bought at the bakery — half croissant, half beignet, entirely excessive, completely right for the occasion. Everything else, the careful sourcing, the slow caramelizing, the balanced cocktail, was decoration around what her mother had always called the **meat and potatoes** of a good table: people hungry and a little impatient, reaching past each other for more.
:::
